script: Your dog greets you like you've been gone for years, even if you only stepped out to get the mail. And it turns out there's real science behind that devotion. When dogs and their owners look into each other's eyes, both of them get a rise in oxytocin, the same bonding hormone that connects parents and babies. Researchers believe this loop developed over thousands of years of living alongside people, and it's one reason dogs are so tuned in to our faces, our voices and our moods. Dogs have also been shaped by selective breeding to pay close attention to humans, which is why even young puppies can follow a pointing finger, something wolves find much harder. On top of that, you provide food, safety, play and routine, and dogs are very good at linking those good things to you personally. Brain scans even show strong reward responses in dogs when they smell their own owner. So when your dog melts at the sight of you, it's not just habit, it's a genuine bond that goes both ways. The more calm, consistent time you spend together, especially through training and play, the stronger that bond becomes.
